query: Consider the following context: High-temperature self-lubricating materials with stable tribological performance across a wide temperature range are essential for advanced mechanical systems under extreme conditions. However, balancing mechanical strength and lubrication efficiency remains a key challenge. In that context, which material can be used for high-performance wide-temperature self-lubricating materials, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) engineered with stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs) and a minor addition of designable lubricious phases can serve as a high-performance, wide-temperature self‐lubricating material by maintaining ultrahigh strength while reducing friction at elevated temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: A tungsten refractory high-entropy alloy processed to exhibit ultrahigh strength and ductility via SCCPs.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor lubricious phase into the alloy (or modify the alloy composition) during processing so that self-lubricating nanoprecipitates are formed in tandem with the SCCP structure.
generation.conditions: Operation under tribological loading over a wide temperature range (from ambient temperature up to 800 °C or higher) in high-stress, high-temperature environments.
generation.structural_mediator: Coherent nanoprecipitates that not only strengthen the alloy (by facilitating dislocation transmission) but also act as reservoirs or localized sources of lubrication at the sliding interfaces.
generation.mechanism: The lubricious nanoprecipitates lower the interfacial friction by creating a self-adaptive lubrication layer during sliding, while the SCCP-mediated microstructure maintains mechanical integrity by relieving stress concentrations and facilitating dislocation movement.
generation.predicted_outcome: The alloy is expected to retain an ultrahigh strength (e.g., >2 GPa) and exhibit a reduced friction coefficient and lower wear rate across the tested temperature range compared to similar tungsten-based alloys without the engineered lubricious phase.
generation.baseline: A tungsten-based refractory alloy lacking the specifically introduced lubricious nanoprecipitates (i.e., the same RHEA with only SCCPs).
generation.boundary: Performance may be affected in environments where the temperature exceeds the stability limit of the lubricious phase or under aggressive chemical conditions that degrade the lubricious component.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative impact of the lubricious phase on friction reduction and its interplay with the SCCPs structure, as well as the long-term stability under cyclic high-temperature tribological conditions, remains to be fully determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of samples: one tungsten-based RHEA with the engineered self-lubricating nanoprecipitates and one control sample without the lubricious phase. Conduct tribological tests (e.g., wear and friction tests) across a range of temperatures (room temperature to >800 °C) under identical normal loads.
measurements: Wear rate via mass loss or surface profilometry
Retention of tensile strength and ductility
Microstructural analysis (e.g., TEM/SEM) pre- and post-testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified RHEA does not exhibit a statistically significant decrease in friction coefficient and wear rate while maintaining its mechanical integrity compared to the control sample across the target temperature range, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High-performance refractory alloys with ultrahigh strength and ductility are in demand for a wide range of critical applications, such as plasma-facing components. However, it remains challenging to increase the strength of these alloys without seriously compromising their tensile ductility. Here, we put forward a strategy to “defeat” this trade-off in tungsten refractory high-entropy alloys by stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitations (SCCPs). The coherent interfaces of SCCPs facilitate the dislocation transmission and relieve the stress concentrations that can lead to premature crack initiation. As a consequence, our alloy displays an ultrahigh strength of 2.15 GPa with a tensile ductility of 15% at ambient temperature, with a high yield strength of 1.05 GPa at 800 °C. The SCCPs design concept may afford a means to develop a wide range of ultrahigh-strength metallic materials by providing a pathway for alloy design. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical engineering

Materials with high performance both at room and elevated temperatures are very attractive for a wide range of critical applications, potentially for aero-engine and fusion reactors [1] – [4] . For decades, ultra-strong, ductile, and heat-resistant materials have long been sought by the materials community, such as tungsten-based heavy alloys and nickel-based superalloys [3] , [5] . However, achieving alloys with an ultrahigh strength (>2 GPa) and a sufficient ductility (>10%) has presented a long-standing challenge. This has spurred significant research into metallurgical strategies to tailor microstructures for improved properties. One classical design paradigm is utilizing dilute concentrations of alloying elements, such as Re, Ti, and Cr, to improve the properties of W-based alloys; however, the “strength-ductility trade-off” has proven to be difficult to be solved with such single principal-element alloy systems due to the problem of brittle W-enriched phases with body-centered cubic (bcc) structures [5] , [6] .
